parakeet: Instead of responding to what science actually says, critics swap it out for a weaker, more ridiculous version. They argue against that instead. And because the replacement is easier to knock down, it creates the illusion of victory without ever touching the real argument. Once you recognize this move, it becomes hard to unsee. You start noticing how often science is not being debated, but impersonated, misrepresented in order to be defeated. And that realization alone should make us pause before taking most science versus religion arguments at face value. Another claim that shows up constantly in these conversations goes something like this. Science keeps changing, so how can it be trusted? At first glance, that sounds reasonable. Stability feels trustworthy. Consistency feels safe. But this argument only works if you quietly assume that science is trying to function the same way that religion does. It isn't. Religion makes absolute claims and then asks people to organize their lives around loyalty to those claims. The expectation is preservation, holding the belief steady, defending it, passing it down unchanged. And that framework change looks like failure. Science operates on a completely different logic. Science does not begin with conclusions, it begins with questions. It does not offer doctrine, it builds models. And those models are provisional by design. They're meant to be tested, challenged, refined, or discarded as new evidence becomes available.
